source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: a Many Labs replication project (manuscript PDF from OSF project wx7ck)
finding: Primary Many Labs 1 manuscript. Gain-loss framing (Asian disease, US replaced by country of data collection, word Asian dropped) replicated in about 31 of 36 samples in the predicted direction and significant; none reversed.
numbers: 36 samples, 6,344 participants in total; framing test chi2(1)=516.4, N=6,271, p<.001. Original ES 1.13 [.89,1.37]. Replication ES in the table: median .58, then .62 [.52,.71] and .60 [.53,.67] (column labels garbled in the PDF text). Proportion of samples: 0.00 opposite significant, 0.86 same-direction significant, 0.14 not significant.
limits: Table layout lost in text extraction, so which of .62 and .60 is weighted versus unweighted is not certain; the supplement text gives d=.60. The original ES of 1.13 is the manuscript's own estimate.
agent_relevance: Closes the human anchor gap: the effect is large in humans but about half the original size. Use d about 0.6 as the human benchmark for agent flip rates.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs 1 web supplement (ML.web.Supplement.pdf)
finding: Gives the raw percentages for the Asian disease replication next to the 1981 originals.
numbers: Original: 72% chose sure Program A, 28% risky B; loss frame 22% chose sure C, 78% risky D. Replication: 62.2% A, 37.8% B; loss frame 33.5% C, 66.5% D. chi2(1)=516.41, p<.0001, d=.60. 73 subjects failed to give a valid answer.
quote: In Condition 2 this effect was reversed, as Program C (400 people die) was adopted by only 33.5% percent while 66.5% percent selected Program D
limits: Sure-option share fell from 72% to 62.2% in gain and rose from 22% to 33.5% in loss, so the swing shrank from 50 points to 28.7 points. Wording changed (country name, no Asian).
agent_relevance: The human flip is a swing of about 29 points, not a full reversal; a model that swings 30-40 points is human-sized, not extreme.

source: Steiger and Kuhberger (2018) A meta-analytic re-appraisal of the framing effect (Zeitschrift fur Psychologie 226(1)), abstract via Crossref
finding: Re-analysis of Kuhberger 1998 with p-curve to correct for publication bias gives a larger, not smaller, effect. Authors conclude there is no replicability crisis for risky-choice framing.
numbers: Kuhberger 1998 overall d=0.31; p-curve corrected d=0.52; Many Labs gain-loss framing d=0.60; new meta-analysis of risk-framing experiments published in 2016 gave d=0.56. No evidence of intense p-hacking.
quote: there is no doubt about their existence: risky-choice framing effects are highly reliable and robust. No replicability crisis there.
limits: Only the abstract was readable (publisher full text returned 403). Moderators differ, so there is no single risky-choice effect. The 0.52 re-uses Kuhberger's study set.
agent_relevance: Raises the human reference from d=0.31 to about 0.5-0.6; corrects the earlier claim that the pooled effect is only small to moderate.

source: Pinon and Gambara (2005) A meta-analytic review of framing effect: risky, attribute and goal framing (Psicothema 17(2))
finding: Full text extracted this session. Meta-analysis of studies from 1997-2003 (after Kuhberger's window). Risky-choice framing is a medium effect, attribute framing is smaller, goal framing equals risky.
numbers: 51 independent studies, 151 effect sizes, nearly 13,500 subjects. d=0.437 risky, 0.260 attribute, 0.444 goal. Heterogeneity significant (p<.0001). Asian disease was the task in 47.7% of cases; 88.7% between-subjects; 83.4% student samples. Risky-choice effect sizes: k=87.
limits: Many moderators; a regression with 7 variables had R2=0.465. Some subsets are tiny (k=4 or 5).
agent_relevance: Confirms d about 0.44 and that attribute framing (admit/reject, mortality vs survival) is a different, smaller effect than risky choice. LLM studies that use attribute framing (Echterhoff, Knipper, FrameBench) should not be pooled with Asian-disease numbers.

source: Talboy and Fuller (2023) Challenging the appearance of machine intelligence: cognitive bias in LLMs and best practices for adoption (arXiv 2304.01358)
finding: The framing section is a one-shot qualitative demonstration with ChatGPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Bard. All three chose one program in the positive frame and the opposite in the negative frame at first testing. Bard answered consistently when retested in August 2023.
numbers: No counts, no repeats, no percentages. Three models, two sessions (spring and August 2023), one prompt per frame.
quote: all three models were susceptible to this effect during initial testing
limits: The paper has no primary numbers for framing. It cannot be cited as a rate. The answer to the gap is: none exist.
agent_relevance: Treat as an anecdote only. It also notes the models gave long, confident reasons for each opposite choice, which matters for any 'ask the model to explain' safeguard.

source: Wang and Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent LLMs: a cross-family behavioral analysis (arXiv 2603.19282)
finding: Full text read. Two threshold-voting prompts told as survival stories (individual versus collective wording) give very different Option B rates across 82 models.
numbers: 82 models, 11 families, 20 trials each. 3,280 classified responses, 1,640 per scenario. Scenario A: 1,472 A, 70 B, 98 non-compliant, so B=4.3% of 1,640. Scenario B: 346 A, 1,128 B, 166 non-compliant, so B=68.8% of 1,640. Among valid answers only: 4.5% and 76.5%.
limits: The 4.3% and 68.8% use all responses as denominator, including non-compliant ones. The two prompts differ in text beyond a frame (instrumental versus cooperative story) and their claimed logical equivalence is arguable. Not a gain-loss risky choice. Family totals pool models by summing counts.
agent_relevance: Shows a story wording can swing parallel same-prompt agents far more than a human framing effect. Do not cite it as gain-loss framing.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley and He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (arXiv 2403.00811v3), Table 3
finding: Full text read. Admission-decision attribute framing (admit versus reject wording of the same student). GPT-4 flips opposite to humans; GPT-3.5 in the human direction. Awareness, contrastive and counterfactual prompts did not fix GPT-4. A model-written neutral rewrite (selfhelp) did.
numbers: Dataset of 13,465 prompts. Admit rate admit-frame / reject-frame: GPT-3.5 baseline .685/.520 (delta +.165); GPT-4 baseline .375/.780 (delta -.405). GPT-4 awareness delta -.470, contrastive -.410, counterfactual -.570, selfhelp -.010. GPT-3.5 selfhelp delta -.080. After selfhelp 2.7% of GPT-4 framing prompts remain biased; Llama-2 13B 0%, 7B 1.4%. Awareness cut biased GPT-3.5 framing prompts to 17.2%.
limits: Attribute framing in admissions, not risky choice. Models are 2023-2024 (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2). Selfhelp for other biases works only on high-capacity models. Not at equal tokens; no canonical-table arm.
agent_relevance: Direct support that a model-written neutral rewrite can remove a framing gap in a strong model, while 'be aware' prompts can make it worse. Sets the baseline a code-run canonical form must beat.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in large language models (arXiv 2508.00902)
finding: Full text read. Reasoning-class models (o3, Claude-4-Thinking) still show framing effects on three-option story scenarios: large in sport, moderate in border and maritime military cases, reversed in career, near zero in business and trade.
numbers: 5 models, 25 iterations per condition, 2,550 decisions. Risk score 0-2, effect = loss minus gain. Championship strategy: o3 +1.640, Claude-4 +1.800, Claude-4-Thinking +1.680, GPT-4o +1.840, Gemini-1.5-Pro +1.400. Career transition: o3 -0.480, Claude-4-Thinking -0.600. Business: o3 +0.080 (p=0.3984), Claude-4-Thinking -0.240 (p=0.0102). Mann-Whitney p<0.05 for o3 in 4 of 7 scenarios (career, championship, maritime, border) and Claude-4-Thinking in 6 of 7 (all but trade route).
limits: No same-wording repeat baseline other than the within-cell spread used in the Mann-Whitney test. 25 runs per cell. Gemini 2.5 Pro left out because it refused military scenarios. Mid-2025 model snapshots. Three-option design, not two.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly yes: a reasoning-class model flips beyond within-cell noise in at least 4 of 7 story scenarios across civilian and geopolitical domains. Domain decides the size and even the sign.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Same probabilities, different advice: gain-loss framing effects in high-stakes LLM decision support (FrameBench-HPS, arXiv 2610.29294), main results
finding: Full text read. 240 scenarios in four domains (healthcare, finance, education/career, legal/consumer rights), 2,880 prompts, 7 models at temperature 0. Gain versus loss wording of the same probability changes the recommendation category far more than repeating the same wording.
numbers: Category change in 32.41% of complete groups; direct yes/no reversals only 0.63%; 98.1% of 2,153 changes involve the 'uncertain' category. Model rates (text): GPT-4o-mini 63.33%, GPT-5 33.40%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 32.56%, GPT-4.1-mini 29.17%, Gemini 3 Flash 23.38%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 22.81%, Qwen3-VL-235B 21.58%. Robustness subset (32 scenarios, 3 models, 3 repeats): same-frame repeat disagreement 7.12% [5.56-8.68] versus cross-frame 34.32% [31.45-37.09]; per-model matched-repeat change GPT-4o-mini 56.5%, Sonnet 4.6 32.0%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 14.1%. Risk shift falls with probability: 0.535 at 20%, 0.287 at 40%, 0.209 at 60%, 0.109 at 80%.
limits: Advice recommendation, not an explicit sure-versus-gamble choice. No per-domain breakdown found in the text I read. The Appendix model table is scrambled in the PDF text, so per-model figures come from the main text. Noise baseline is pooled over three models; it was not measured for GPT-5. Gemini 2.5 Pro shows 32.56% on the full set but 14.1% on the subset.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly: a reasoning-class model (GPT-5) changes category in 33.4% of groups against a pooled noise floor of 7.12%, so the flip is far above repeat noise, but model-specific noise and per-domain results are missing.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) FrameBench-HPS interventions (arXiv 2610.29294), section 5.3 and Appendix
finding: Full text check of the canonicalization numbers. Canonicalization is one sentence stating both complementary probabilities, put into the prompt. Frame-robust prompting is an instruction prepended to the prompt. No code-run table, no model-written rewrite arm, no token matching.
numbers: Matched-repeat category change: conversational baseline 34.20%, original templates 36.81%, canonicalization 6.68% [5.12-8.51], frame-robust instruction 22.83% [19.88-25.87]. Paired reduction by canonicalization 27.52 points [24.13-30.82]. Risk shift 0.363 to -0.010; confidence gap 0.477 to 0.145; direct reversals 0.35% (canonical) and 1.56% (instruction). 3 models (GPT-4o-mini, Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro), 32 held-out scenarios, 2,304 responses per condition.
quote: Probability canonicalization explicitly presents both complementary probabilities in a common representation.
limits: The canonical text adds one sentence, so token cost is about the same as the instruction arm, but this was not measured or matched. Single stated probabilities only. Direct reversals rose slightly under the instruction.
agent_relevance: The numbers in claim K12 are confirmed in full text. Gap 1 stays open: the three-way test (code-run canonical table versus self-rewrite versus instruction) was not run by anyone I found.

source: Pilli and Nallur (2026) Predicting biased human decision-making with LLMs in conversational settings (arXiv 2601.11049v2)
finding: Pre-registered human study (N=1,648) with a demanding versus a simple chatbot dialogue before the choice. Humans show a bigger risky-choice framing effect after the complex dialogue. LLMs asked to play the participant (given the same dialogue) also show a larger effect after the complex dialogue under two of three prompt styles.
numbers: Humans, risky-choice framing, Cohen's h: simple dialogue 0.205 [-0.001, 0.410], complex dialogue 0.730 [0.524, 0.937]; z of the difference 3.53. LLM role-play effect size, simple to complex: HL1 1.770 to 2.447 (z 4.53), HL2 1.252 to 2.299 (z 7.04), HL3 0.690 to 0.810 (z 0.81, not significant). Prediction accuracy for risky choice .52 choice-only, .62 no dialogue, .60 with dialogue (n=177).
limits: The LLM is predicting a human's pick as a persona, not answering for itself. Its role-play effects are 3 to 9 times the human size. Dialogue added nothing to individual accuracy for risky choice. The model behind each Table 4 column was not confirmed (Table 3 uses GPT-4.1). Context was a chat about music taste, not raw padding.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly answered: in role-play, longer demanding context raised the simulated frame effect in 2 of 3 prompt styles. Whether the agent's own judgment drifts with long irrelevant context is still untested.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The bias is in the details: an assessment of cognitive bias in LLMs (arXiv 2509.22856)
finding: 45 LLMs, over 2.8 million responses, eight biases. Reasoning-trained models resisted framing better than size-matched ordinary models. More detailed prompts helped a little for framing.
numbers: Framing resistance score (higher is better): QwQ-32B .818 versus Qwen2.5-32B .602; DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-32B .865; DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-14B .826 versus Qwen2.5-14B .365; DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B .717 versus Llama-3.3-70B .697; R1-Llama-8B .705 versus cogito-8B .642; Phi-3.5-mini .262. By prompt detail level (TELeR L1 to L5): .473, .509, .561, .538, .549. Authors: framing 'uniquely benefits from intermediate reasoning steps'.
limits: Template items such as 11% mortality versus 83% success for two surgeons: attribute framing, not Asian disease. Reasoning models differ from base models in training, not only in thinking at test time. Open models up to 72B; the frontier closed models are not in this table.
agent_relevance: Contradicts the small-model result that chain-of-thought raised flips (28.6% to 57.1%). Gap 9 is split: reasoning-trained 14-70B models are more frame-resistant on attribute items, prompted CoT in 7-8B models was not. Frontier models on risky choice remain untested head to head.

source: Ge, Zhang and Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) gap! A contrast in risky choices between reasoning and conversational LLMs (arXiv 2602.15173v2), framing results
finding: Full text read. 20 LLMs plus matched human subjects on explicit two-option money prospects. Reasoning models are close to expected-value maximisers and ignore gain/loss framing and option order. Conversational models are strongly framing-sensitive.
numbers: Correlation of reasoning models with the risk-neutral reference 0.86 to 1; conversational models below 0.5. Humans nearly uncorrelated with the reference; highest LLM-human correlation 0.42 (Claude Haiku). Humans are 'considerably less influenced by gain/loss framing than CMs'. Temperature T=1; humans via Prolific; three base prospect pairs.
limits: Prospects are explicit numeric gambles with matched expected value, so a reasoning model can compute and win. Does not transfer automatically to story scenarios (see d08 and d09).
agent_relevance: Supports: explicit numbers plus a model that computes expected value removes the flip. The agent should force that computation path.

source: Ge, Zhang and Vorobeychik (2026) explanation findings (arXiv 2602.15173v2), sections 1 and 5
finding: Asking for a one-sentence or a mathematical explanation changes decisions for all models, more for conversational models. Brief explanations moved models closer to the risk-neutral reference than no explanation or a math explanation.
numbers: Stated finding 3: 'Explanations impact decisions for all models'. Qwen3-30B-Thinking and Olmo3-32B-Think change significantly under math explanation, with no difference between no explanation and brief explanation. Per-model test values were not fully extracted from the PDF.
limits: Not a chain-of-thought on/off test on frontier models. Explanations here are an output instruction, not hidden reasoning. Only the summary statements and part of section 5 were read.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: a short rationale does not hurt and may help in explicit-prospect tasks; the effect is not stable across reasoning models.

source: Payne (2025) mathematical control experiment (arXiv 2508.00902, section 4.4 and Table 8)
finding: When the same options are given in pure symbolic form and the model must compute expected values, the framing effect disappears for both GPT-4o and o3.
numbers: o3: 200/200 (100%) success and 200/200 (100%) declarations of indifference across loss-prevention and gain-achievement frames; text says GPT-4o also expressed indifference in 100% of cases. Rationale coding: o3 calculated EV correctly about 85% of the time in military scenarios, yet still showed the narrative frame effect.
limits: Symbolic scenarios are abstract and short; they remove the story entirely, so this is an upper bound for a canonical rewrite. Framing effect size was not significantly correlated with how often rationales calculated EV. Table 7 (EV calculation rates by scenario) was scrambled in extraction and is not quoted.
agent_relevance: Best available evidence for the code-style canonicalization idea: strip semantics, compute, then answer. Also shows that 'the model did the arithmetic' is not enough; it must decide from the arithmetic.
